title: Determining wavelength with a diffraction grating
prior_knowledge_summary: Lesson 10 established d sin θ = nλ, conversion from ruling density to grating spacing, order number and symmetric maxima.
Earlier wave learning established wavelength and the need for single-frequency light when one wavelength is to be measured.
new_learning: Describe a complete diffraction-grating method for determining wavelength.
Use repeated symmetric angular measurements, averaging and d sin θ = nλ to determine wavelength.
Explain how symmetry and repetition improve the measurement.

blocks.title: One colour, two slightly different angles
content: A grating produces the same third-order maximum on the left and right of the centre. A student reads 28.4° on one side and 28.8° on the other. Which angle should be used to find the wavelength?

The pattern should be symmetric, but alignment and reading errors can shift individual readings. The experiment becomes more reliable when we measure a complete left-to-right separation and repeat it instead of trusting one side.

figure.purpose: Create the need for symmetric and repeated angular measurements.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch with a grating at the centre, a straight-through maximum, matching third-order rays left and right, and small reading cards 28.4 degrees and 28.8 degrees. Use sparse coloured marker lines and a question mark, with no calculation.
figure.alt_text: Matching third-order maxima give slightly different one-sided angular readings.

blocks.title: What must be measured

definition.displayed_content: the minimum distance between two adjacent points on a wave that are in phase

content: Use single-frequency light incident normally on a diffraction grating whose ruling density or spacing is known. Identify the central maximum and choose the same order n on both sides. Measure the angle between those two matching maxima.

This is the formula to remember: d sin θ = nλ. Here d is the separation of adjacent grating lines in metres, θ is the angle from the central direction to one maximum, n is the order number and λ is the wavelength in metres. If a ruling density N is supplied, first use d = 1/N with consistent units.

The structure and operation of a spectrometer are outside this lesson and outside the syllabus requirement. The required physics is selecting the maxima, measuring their angular separation and processing those measurements.

figure.purpose: Identify the complete in-scope measurement geometry without teaching spectrometer construction.
figure.brief: Rectangular plan-view teacher diagram showing normal incidence on a grating, central maximum, matching order n maxima and the full angular separation alpha between them. Label theta on each half and alpha equals 2 theta. Show only a generic angular scale, not a spectrometer.
figure.alt_text: The separation between matching order maxima is twice the one-sided diffraction angle.

blocks.title: A complete measurement sequence
content: First direct single-frequency light normally at the grating. Locate the central maximum and matching maxima of a clearly identified order n on the left and right.

Record the angular reading for the left maximum and then for its matching right maximum. Subtract the readings to obtain their separation α. Repeat the left-right pair measurement several times, returning to each maximum independently. Calculate each separation, find the mean separation, then use θ = mean α / 2.
Convert the known ruling density to d if needed. Finally calculate λ = d sin θ / n and state the answer with a suitable unit and significant figures.

figure.purpose: Make the complete experimental and calculation sequence memorable.
figure.brief: Rectangular six-step hand-drawn flow: normal incidence, locate centre, choose matching order, read left and right repeatedly, average separations and halve, calculate lambda. Use numbered boxes, arrows and a small consistent colour palette.
figure.alt_text: A six-step route turns repeated symmetric angle readings into wavelength.

blocks.title: From repeated pairs to one best angle
content: For the second-order maxima, three measured left-to-right separations are 42.6°, 42.9° and 42.7°. The mean separation is (42.6 + 42.9 + 42.7)/3 = 42.733...°, so θ = 21.366...°.
A 600 lines mm⁻¹ grating has d = 10⁻³/600 = 1.6667 × 10⁻⁶ m. Then λ = d sin θ / n = (1.6667 × 10⁻⁶) sin 21.366...° / 2 = 3.036 × 10⁻⁷ m, or 304 nm to three significant figures.
A reverse check gives sin θ = 2(3.036 × 10⁻⁷)/(1.6667 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.3643 and θ = 21.37°, agreeing with the processed angle.

figure.purpose: Show how raw repeated pair measurements become the angle used in the equation.
figure.brief: Rectangular annotated calculation table with three separation readings, mean separation, halving to theta, reciprocal conversion to d, and final lambda substitution. Colour-code measured, processed and calculated quantities.
figure.alt_text: Three symmetric separations are averaged and halved before wavelength is calculated.

blocks.title: Why symmetry, repetition and higher order help
content: Measuring from a left maximum to its right partner uses the full angle 2θ. Halving that separation makes the centre the midpoint, so a small zero-direction offset does not control the result. Repeating independent settings reveals scatter and lets a mean reduce random variation.

It feels reasonable to measure one side repeatedly without moving away because the display looks stable. That can repeat the same alignment bias rather than test it. Re-find both maxima for each pair and keep the order the same.

A higher available order usually gives a larger angle and a larger left-right separation. For the same absolute angular reading uncertainty, a larger measured separation has a smaller percentage uncertainty. The chosen order must still exist, be visible and be identified unambiguously.

figure.purpose: Contrast weak one-sided practice with a stronger repeated symmetric method.
figure.brief: Rectangular comparison panel. Left shows repeated readings of one maximum without re-setting, labelled same bias can remain. Right shows fresh left-right pairs, a mean separation and midpoint. Add a small comparison of narrow first-order versus wider third-order separation.
figure.alt_text: Fresh symmetric pairs and a larger usable order improve angular measurement quality.

blocks.title: Estimate uncertainty from the repeated separations
content: Suppose repeated separations are 61.2°, 61.6°, 61.4° and 61.3°. Their mean is 61.375°. A simple half-range estimate for the uncertainty in one mean separation is (61.6 - 61.2)/2 = 0.2°.

Because θ is half the separation, θ = 30.6875° and its corresponding half-range uncertainty is 0.1°. The spread is small compared with the angle, which supports reporting the wavelength to about three significant figures rather than many calculator digits.

This estimate describes random scatter in the repeated angular settings. It does not prove that the grating spacing is exact or remove a persistent alignment error, so the method and apparatus still need careful alignment.

figure.purpose: Give uncertainty reasoning a visual link to the spread of repeated readings.
figure.brief: Rectangular number-line sketch from 61.2 to 61.6 degrees with four reading marks, mean at 61.375 degrees, half-range 0.2 degrees, then an arrow showing theta and its uncertainty are both halved.
figure.alt_text: The half-range of repeated separations estimates scatter, and halving the separation halves its angular uncertainty.

blocks.title: The full wavelength route
content: Known grating, normal incidence, matching order, repeated left-right separations, mean, halve, then λ = d sin θ / n. Keep angles in degrees on a degree-mode calculator and d and λ in metres during substitution.

Check that both maxima have the same order, the one-sided angle was obtained by halving the pair separation, and the wavelength is plausible for the stated light. Symmetry controls the centre, repetition exposes scatter and the equation converts the best angle into wavelength.

figure.purpose: Consolidate the method, calculation and checks as one final decision map.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper checklist with three columns: measure, process, check. Include matching order and repeated pair readings; mean alpha and theta equals alpha over two; convert d, calculate lambda, verify order, symmetry, unit and plausibility.
figure.alt_text: A final checklist connects measurement, processing and validation of a grating wavelength result.

visual_rules.style: colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch on rectangular white paper

misconceptions_addressed: The angle between matching maxima is θ.
Repeating without independently re-setting removes alignment bias.
A higher order is always preferable even if it is not visible or identifiable.
